Get peak list

Source: R/get_peaks.R
get_peaks.Rd

Detects chromatographic peaks, fits peak models, and extracts peak parameters at one or more wavelengths.

Usage

get_peaks(
  chrom_list,
  lambdas,
  fit = c("egh", "bemg", "gaussian", "raw"),
  windows = NULL,
  targets = NULL,
  tol = 0.1,
  select_by = c("height", "proximity", "none"),
  mod_list = NULL,
  sd_max = NULL,
  max_iter = 1000,
  time_unit = NULL,
  baseline = c("none", "flat", "sloped"),
  estimate_purity = FALSE,
  purity_args = list(),
  show_progress = NULL,
  cl = 2,
  collapse = FALSE,
  time.units = NULL,
  sd.max = NULL,
  max.iter = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

chrom_list

A list of chromatograms in matrix format (timepoints × wavelengths).

lambdas

A character or numeric vector specifying the wavelengths to find peaks at. Omit for one-dimensional chromatograms, or when targets has a lambda column.

fit

Peak model. Options are bidirectional exponentially modified Gaussian ("bemg"), exponential-Gaussian hybrid ("egh"), "gaussian", or "raw". "raw" integrates the signal directly by trapezoidal approximation without fitting a model. Defaults to "egh", or to "raw" when windows is provided, which allows no other value. See Peak models.

windows

Optional two-column matrix or data.frame of start and end retention times (or a single pair of times), giving manual integration windows applied to every chromatogram. If provided, peak detection is skipped and each window is integrated in every sample. Requires fit = "raw". Cannot be combined with targets. Defaults to NULL. See Manual integration windows.

targets

Target retention times, as a numeric vector or a table of targets (see targeted_analysis). If provided, only peaks whose apex falls within tol of a target are fit, and get_peaktable groups peaks by target instead of clustering them. A lambda column replaces lambdas, and a tol column replaces the tol argument, which must then be omitted. Defaults to NULL, which fits every detected peak.

tol

Numeric. The maximum distance between a peak's apex and its target in targets, in minutes, regardless of the time unit of chrom_list. Give one value for all targets, or one per target. Defaults to 0.1. Ignored if targets is NULL.

select_by

Character. Which peak to keep when more than one falls in a target's window: "height" (the default) keeps the most intense, "proximity" the one closest to the target, and "none" all of them. Ignored if targets is NULL.

mod_list

Optional warping models from correct_rt (with what = "models"). If provided, the times in targets are read on the aligned time axis, so they can be copied from the rt row of an aligned peak table. Peaks are still detected and fitted on the unaligned data; use correct_peaks afterwards to add corrected retention times. Requires targets.

sd_max

Deprecated. Filter peaks by width with filter_peaks instead, using min_fwhm and max_fwhm. A standard deviation in timepoints, converted to a FWHM cutoff of 2.355 * sd_max * dt in the units of time_unit, where dt is the chromatogram's time step; wider peaks are discarded. NULL disables width filtering. Ignored if windows is provided.

max_iter

Maximum number of iterations for non-linear least squares in fit_peaks. Defaults to 1000.

time_unit

Units for sd, FWHM, tau, tau_right, tau_left, and area. Options are minutes ("min"), seconds ("s"), or milliseconds ("ms"). Defaults to the time unit of chrom_list (minutes if none is recorded). rt, start and end are not converted: they stay in the units of the chromatogram's own time axis. ChemStation reports areas with time in seconds, so use "s" to compare with it.

baseline

Whether to measure each peak above a local baseline: "none" (the default), "flat" (a constant offset per peak), or "sloped" (an offset that varies linearly across the peak). See Local baselines.

estimate_purity

Logical. Whether to estimate purity. Defaults to FALSE. When TRUE, calls get_purity for every peak in every sample, at a cost that grows with the number of wavelengths.

purity_args

A named list of additional arguments passed to get_purity, e.g. list(background_correction = "none", metric = "max"). A lambdas element here selects the wavelengths used to compare spectra, not the wavelengths at which peaks are integrated.

show_progress

Logical. Whether to show progress bar. Defaults to TRUE if pbapply is installed.

cl

Number of cores (integer) or a cluster object from makeCluster. Defaults to 2. On Windows, only a cluster object runs in parallel; an integer runs serially.

collapse

Logical. Whether to combine the peaks from every wavelength into a single data.frame per sample. Defaults to FALSE.

time.units

The time.units argument is deprecated. Please use time_unit instead.

sd.max

The sd.max argument is deprecated. Please use sd_max instead.

max.iter

The max.iter argument is deprecated. Please use max_iter instead.

...

Additional arguments passed to find_peaks, such as smooth_window, smooth_type, min_prominence_snr, min_curvature and min_amplitude. See Choosing the smoothing window in find_peaks.

Value

An S3 object of class peak_list: a nested list (sample, then wavelength) of data.frames, or a list of one data.frame per sample when collapse = TRUE, with one row per peak and columns:

  • rt: The retention time of the peak maximum. For the fitted models it generally falls between timepoints, so match it to the time axis with a tolerance rather than == or match(); get_spectra with what = "rt" returns the spectrum at the nearest timepoint.

  • start: The retention time where the peak is estimated to begin.

  • end: The retention time where the peak is estimated to end.

  • sd: The standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) of the Gaussian component of the fitted peak shape. This is a parameter of the model rather than the width of the peak: for "egh" and "bemg" the asymmetry of the peak is carried by tau or by tau_left/tau_right, so \(\sigma\) describes only the core of the peak and is not comparable across values of fit. Use FWHM to compare widths. NA when fit = "raw", which fits no model; the width of the integration window is available as end - start.

  • tau: Empirical skewness parameter (in units of time) determining peak asymmetry when fit == "egh".

  • tau_right: Time constant (in units of time) of the exponential tail on the right side of the peak when fit = "bemg". A larger value gives a longer tail, and a value near 0 means no tail on that side.

  • tau_left: Time constant (in units of time) of the exponential tail on the left side of the peak when fit = "bemg". A larger value gives a longer tail, and a value near 0 means no tail on that side.

  • h: The amplitude parameter of the fitted BEMG shape function (only when fit = "bemg"). It scales the shape but is not its value at center, so use the height column for the height of the peak.

  • center: The center parameter of the fitted BEMG shape function (only when fit = "bemg"). This is the location around which the exponential tails are applied. Because BEMG peaks can be asymmetric (tau_right != tau_left) and a sloped baseline shifts the fitted curve, the actual peak maximum (rt) may differ from center.

  • FWHM: The full width at half maximum of the peak. For "gaussian" this is \(2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\,\sigma \approx 2.355 \sigma\); for "egh" it is the closed form \(\sqrt{(\tau\ln 2)^2 + 8\sigma^2\ln 2}\) implied by the model (Lan & Jorgenson, 2001); and for "bemg", which has no closed form, it is measured numerically from the fitted shape. For "raw" it is measured directly from the signal above the local baseline, and is NA when the integration window does not fall below half the height of the peak on both sides, as for a peak fused with a neighbor. Unlike sd, FWHM is comparable across values of fit.

  • height: The height of the peak above the fitted baseline.

  • area: The area of the peak above the fitted baseline, estimated by trapezoidal approximation.

  • r.squared: Coefficient of determination (\(R^2\)) of the fitted curve over the peak window, 1 - SS_res / SS_tot. Negative when the fit is worse than a flat line at the mean. Not returned when fit = "raw".

  • purity: The peak purity as estimated by get_purity. NA unless estimate_purity = TRUE.

  • window_limited: 1 if a fitted shape parameter hit a limit set by the integration window, or a "gaussian" or "egh" fit narrowed to one sampling interval at half height, meaning the window or the sampling rather than the data determined the reported shape, and 0 otherwise. Not returned when fit = "raw".

  • converged: 1 if the nonlinear least squares optimizer reported convergence for the final stage of the fit, and 0 otherwise. A 0 means the reported parameters are wherever the optimizer stopped rather than a converged fit, so treat the corresponding height and area with caution. It also covers the case where part or all of the fit was skipped because the integration window holds too few points to determine it; the peak then keeps the last step that ran, or its starting values (see Fitting procedure). get_peaks warns when more than 20% of peaks sit in such a window. Not returned when fit = "raw".

  • floor: Constant baseline level (only when baseline = "flat").

  • floor_start: Baseline level at the left edge of the peak window (only when baseline = "sloped").

  • floor_end: Baseline level at the right edge of the peak window (only when baseline = "sloped"). For the peak models, floor, floor_start and floor_end are constrained to be non-negative.

  • target: The row of targets the peak was selected for (only when targets is supplied).

Details

Peaks are detected by find_peaks as zero-crossings in the smoothed first derivative of each trace, then fitted by fit_peaks according to fit (see Peak models and Fitting procedure). Peak areas are the trapezoidal integral of the fitted curve (or, for fit = "raw", of the signal) above the local baseline (see Local baselines). To integrate fixed retention-time ranges instead, see Manual integration windows.

Note

Adapted from getAllPeaks by Ron Wehrens (https://github.com/rwehrens/alsace/blob/master/R/getAllPeaks.R); however, the underlying algorithms for finding and integrating peaks differ.

Peak models

The three peak models are fitted to each peak by nonlinear least squares; "raw" uses no model.

  • "gaussian": a symmetric Gaussian, with a center, a width (sd) and a height.

  • "egh": the exponential-Gaussian hybrid of Lan & Jorgenson (2001), a Gaussian whose width grows on one side of the apex. It adds one parameter, tau, which is positive for a tailing peak and negative for a fronting one.

  • "bemg": the average of two exponentially modified Gaussians, one with an exponential tail to the left and one to the right. Their time constants, tau_left and tau_right, set the two tails independently, so a peak can tail, front, or both; a value near 0 means no tail on that side.

  • "raw": no model. The signal itself is integrated across the window, so r.squared, window_limited and converged are not reported.

"gaussian" cannot follow tailing or fronting; "egh" follows one or the other, but not both in the same peak; "bemg" follows both. The more flexible models have more parameters (3, 4 and 5 respectively for the peak shape, plus one more for a "flat" baseline or two more for a "sloped" baseline).

Local baselines

A peak's height and area are measured over its integration window, which runs from the valley before the peak to the valley after it, as found by find_peaks, or spans the manual window if the windows argument is given.

  • With baseline = "none", height and area are measured from zero, so the chromatogram should already be baseline corrected (see preprocess).

  • With the fitted peak models ("gaussian", "egh", "bemg"), a "flat" or "sloped" baseline is fitted together with the peak shape by nonlinear least squares. It cannot be negative; a flat baseline is capped at the lowest intensity in the window, and each end of a sloped one is capped at the median intensity of the first or last 2% of the window. height and area are those of the fitted shape above the baseline, with the area integrated across the integration window only.

  • With fit = "raw", nothing is fitted: a "flat" baseline is a horizontal line at the lower of the two boundary intensities, and a "sloped" one a straight line between them. Where that line lies above the signal, it subtracts area, so the area can come out negative; get_peaktable records a negative area as 0.

With "flat" or "sloped", each peak gets its own baseline. This differs from drop-line integration in vendor software such as ChemStation, where a vertical line from each valley meets a baseline shared by the whole cluster of peaks.

Fitting procedure

A fit is built up in successive steps: first the peak shape, then a constant baseline, and finally its slope. To fit the full model, a peak's integration window must have at least as many timepoints as there are parameters in the model. A step is skipped if the window has too few timepoints to fit all the required parameters, and discarded if the optimizer cannot start from its initial values or, for "bemg", if a fitted tail rises towards the edge of the window instead of falling back towards the baseline. Either way, the peak keeps the last step that worked. A "sloped" baseline can therefore come out flat, or a baseline can be left at its starting estimate rather than fitted, and if even the shape fails, every parameter will keep its starting value. In each of these cases, converged is set to 0.

Peaks that can't be fitted at all are dropped, unless they come from targets. Those are kept, with height and area set to NA and converged to 0, so that every target found has a row.

Manual integration windows

Manual windows integrate every sample over the same retention-time ranges, so each compound is measured the same way in every sample, and every sample gets the same set of peak table columns. The raw signal in each window is integrated whether or not a peak is detected there, so a window with no peak gets an area near zero. With baseline = "none", two adjacent windows sharing a boundary time act as a vertical drop line: their areas sum exactly to the area of their union, so a peak can be split at a chosen time. The "flat" and "sloped" baselines are drawn within each window separately, so their areas do not sum to that of the union. To fit peak models at known retention times, use targets instead.

  • Naish, P. J. & Hartwell, S. 1988. Exponentially Modified Gaussian functions — A good model for chromatographic peaks in isocratic HPLC? Chromatographia, 26: 285-296. doi:10.1007/BF02268168 .

  • Arase, Shuntaro, Kanta Horie, Takashi Kato, et al. 2016. Intelligent Peak Deconvolution through In-Depth Study of the Data Matrix from Liquid Chromatography Coupled with a Photo-Diode Array Detector Applied to Pharmaceutical Analysis. Journal of Chromatography. A, 1469: 35–47. doi:10.1016/j.chroma.2016.09.037 .

  • O'Haver, Tom. Pragmatic Introduction to Signal Processing: Applications in scientific measurement. https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~toh/spectrum/ (Accessed January, 2022).

  • Wehrens, R., Carvalho, E., Fraser, P.D. 2015. Metabolite profiling in LC–DAD using multivariate curve resolution: the alsace package for R. Metabolomics 11:143-154. doi:10.1007/s11306-014-0683-5 .

Examples

data(Sa_pr)
pks <- get_peaks(Sa_pr, lambdas = c('210'), fit = "egh")
pks <- filter_peaks(pks, max_fwhm = 1)
